proof:
# Sparse node slacks, rank-controlled polygons, and the quadrilateral row reduction

This is an ordinary planar reconstruction theorem. It preserves prescribed ray endpoints and sector areas exactly. It does not preserve compatibility between different mixed-integer fibers, and it is not a proof of a Lorentz inequality on quadrilaterals.

The finite geometric and PSD equivalence used below is proved in
`candidate 697de064a9368ba1` and
`candidate 2e26c63010f03ffc`.

## 1. A positive solution with one nonzero forcing coordinate

Let C be a real symmetric positive-definite matrix whose off-diagonal entries are nonpositive. Suppose its graph, joining i and j when C_ij<0, is connected. For any chosen index j, the vector

    w=C^{-1}e_j

is strictly positive in every coordinate.

Here is a direct proof, including the assertion of positivity. The strictly convex coercive function

    F(x)=x^T C x/2-x_j

has a unique minimizer w, characterized by Cw=e_j. Replacing x by its coordinatewise absolute value cannot increase the quadratic term, because the off-diagonal coefficients are nonpositive; it cannot increase -x_j either. Uniqueness therefore gives w=|w|, so w>=0.

If w_i=0, then the i-th equation is

    -sum_(l!=i) (-C_il) w_l=(e_j)_i.

The left side is nonpositive. Thus i cannot equal j, and for i!=j all adjacent coordinates must also vanish. Connectivity propagates zeros to j, a contradiction. Hence w>0. A singleton block is included: its positive diagonal gives w_j=1/C_jj>0.

For a connected singular positive-semidefinite matrix with the same sign pattern, a positive kernel vector also exists. Indeed minimize the Rayleigh quotient on the unit sphere, replace a minimizer by absolute values, and use the same zero-propagation argument in the eigenvector equation. Its least eigenvalue is zero. The kernel is one-dimensional: for a positive kernel vector w, conjugating C by diag(w) gives a graph Laplacian with positive edge weights, whose quadratic form vanishes only on constants when the graph is connected. A singular singleton has its single positive vector as kernel.

## 2. Exact prescribed-sector data

Let m>=3 prescribed nonzero ray endpoints P_i be cyclically ordered about zero, with every consecutive angular gap less than pi. Set

    D_i=det(P_i,P_(i+1))>0,
    E_i=det(P_(i-1),P_(i+1)),
    kappa_i=D_(i-1)+D_i-E_i.

Prescribe sector areas W_i>=D_i/2 and define

    t_i=2W_i/D_i>=1,
    a_i=t_i-1,
    h_i=a_i/(D_i t_i)=1/D_i-1/(2W_i)>=0,
    b_i=kappa_i/(D_(i-1)D_i).

Define the symmetric matrix L by

    x^T L x=sum_i b_i x_i^2-sum_i h_i(x_i+x_(i+1))^2.   (1)

By the exact PSD criterion, the data have a convex-body realization with zero in its interior if and only if L is positive semidefinite. A sector with h_i=0 is a core sector. Let p be the number of positive h_i, and assume at least one core sector exists. Then the positive-edge graph is a union of paths and singletons, with exactly m-p connected components. Let s be the number of singular components, and let d_0 be the number of positive-definite components. Thus

    s+d_0=m-p.                                        (2)

All connected singular components have nullity one, by Section 1. Therefore

    rank L=m-s=p+d_0.                                 (3)

The core assumption is important here. If all h_i are positive, the graph is a cycle and p=m; formula (2) does not hold and the rank count below is not asserted.

## 3. Sparse-slack reconstruction

In each singular connected component choose a positive kernel vector. In each positive-definite component choose any one index j and use the vector C^{-1}e_j of Section 1. Concatenating these choices gives a finite vector w>0 with

    Lw>=0,

and with Lw nonzero at exactly ONE index of each positive-definite component and zero at every other index.

For each positive edge use the exact charges

    r_i=h_i(1+w_i/w_(i+1)),
    s_i=h_i(1+w_(i+1)/w_i).

They obey r_i s_i/(r_i+s_i)=h_i. Set both charges to zero at a core edge. The node budget slack is exactly

    delta_i=b_i-r_(i-1)-s_i=(Lw)_i/w_i.                (4)

For h_i>0, put

    u_i=t_i w_(i+1)/(w_i+w_(i+1)),
    v_i=t_i w_i/(w_i+w_(i+1)),
    V_i=u_i P_i+v_i P_(i+1).

For a core edge use u_i=v_i=1/2, so V_i is the midpoint of P_i,P_(i+1). All coefficients are strictly positive and finite. The exact finite convexity theorem reconstructs the polygon with boundary sequence

    P_1,V_1,P_2,V_2,...,P_m,V_m,

allowing straight joins. Its sector areas are exactly W_i and its ray endpoints are exactly P_i.

For completeness, its local turns identify the vertices without any generic-position assumption. At V_i the signed turn is

    det(V_i-P_i,P_(i+1)-V_i)=(t_i-1)D_i,

which is strictly positive precisely on the p positive edges. At P_i, the finite convexity calculation gives

    det(P_i-V_(i-1),V_i-P_i)
       =u_(i-1)v_i D_(i-1)D_i delta_i.                (5)

The prefactor is strictly positive, including at core edges. Hence P_i is a strict vertex precisely at the d_0 chosen indices. All other ray points lie in the relative interiors of straight boundary portions. The source lies in the interior of the reconstructed convex body, so these straight joins do not reverse direction or collapse an entire body to a line.

Consequently the reconstructed polygon has exactly p+d_0 strict vertices, and in particular at most rank L vertices by (3). The identities in fact give equality for this reconstruction. Its data remain the original actual data; no sector area or ray endpoint is perturbed.

**Rank-controlled reconstruction theorem.** If realizable prescribed ray/sector data have at least one core sector, they admit a polygonal realization with rank L vertices. Equivalently, each singular connected block saves one vertex relative to the m prescribed rays. The selected surviving ray vertex in each PD block can be chosen arbitrarily within that block.

## 4. Application to fixed-sector Lorentz-row maxima

Now specialize to the six rays of three fixed balanced spanning planar normals and an interior source. In canonical coordinates the endpoints are

    (A,0),(0,B),(-t,t),(-a,0),(0,-b),(r,-r),

with all six radii positive. For fixed actual six sector areas, the feasible radius set is compact, and every selected generalized Lorentz row attains a maximum. These facts, together with the two structural conclusions used next, are proved in
`candidate 1a5bfc0fdb9108c3`:

1. A row maximum has at least two core sectors.
2. Its positive-edge graph has at least two singular connected blocks.

Both conclusions were proved directly for the selected Lorentz row by exact feasible radius variations, positive-semidefinite block control, and one-coordinate projective curvature. They require no cap ceiling, cap profile, triangle-extremizer assumption, or polygonal approximation of a varying mixed fiber.

Apply Section 3 to the maximizing data. Since m=6 and s>=2, its sparse-slack reconstruction has

    rank L=6-s<=4

vertices. The construction preserves all six maximizing ray endpoints as well as all six original sector areas. Thus it preserves the maximizing row exactly. In particular the replacement has the same total area, the same three cap areas, and every condition expressed in these sector or cap areas. Mapping back from canonical coordinates preserves the corresponding normalizations and row values.

**Global ordinary quadrilateral reduction.** For an arbitrary planar convex body with an interior source and three fixed balanced spanning normals, and for each selected generalized Lorentz row, there exists a triangle or quadrilateral with the same six sector areas and with selected row at least as large. It may be chosen to realize an attained fixed-sector row maximum. No bound on the number of vertices of the original body and no cap-fraction restriction is needed.

The three independent maxima for three different rows need not be realized by the same polygon. No claim to that effect is used. Nor does the replacement preserve any neighboring integer fiber or midpoint inclusion. The inequality on the remaining actual quadrilateral family must still be proved or disproved; the reduction itself supplies no such inequality.

## 5. Relation to the previous pentagon enumeration

The previous least-eigenvector reconstruction gave a vertex at EVERY node of a PD block, and hence counted p plus the number of PD nodes. That count was a valid upper bound but was not optimal. The present construction puts all forcing in one coordinate of each PD block, leaving only one strict ray vertex there. It therefore removes the residual pentagon and Type-B hexagon counts without contradicting their actual realizability: those bodies can have the same finite data as a polygon with fewer vertices.

The independently proved double-core support-triangle and one-corner compression remains a direct geometric description of one branch, but is not needed for the general quadrilateral reduction. The cap-band pentagon and Type-B calculations remain valid in their stated scopes.
